title: As Corporate Bond Markets Grow, Is Bank Lending Shrinking? - Liberty Street Economics
gist: NY Fed researchers decompose growth in corporate bonds-to-GDP across the U.S. and 23 other advanced economies into a shift from bank loans to bonds (composition) versus firms borrowing more overall (credit deepening). U.S. growth since 1996 was mainly credit deepening, the pandemic was a broad borrowing event, and the post-2021 retreat in bonds/GDP is largely a GDP denominator effect rather than a broad return to bank credit.

themes.theme: Bond growth: substitution vs. credit deepening

insights.claim: Rising corporate bonds-to-GDP is usually read as a shift from bank to market finance, but it can equally reflect firms simply borrowing more overall (credit deepening), so the headline ratio alone does not reveal disintermediation.
insights.speaker: Nina Boyarchenko
insights.so_what: Do not infer bank disintermediation from bond-market growth without decomposing it into composition vs. total-debt changes.
insights.quote: This growth is usually read as a shift from bank to market finance. But the ratio of bonds to GDP can rise either because firms take more debt in general, or because firms shift the composition of their debt toward bonds.

insights.claim: If bond markets grow because firms substitute away from banks, bond-market conditions govern a larger share of corporate liabilities and bank lending standards a smaller one; if growth comes from more borrowing of everything, firms are simply more exposed to both channels.
insights.speaker: Nina Boyarchenko
insights.so_what: The source of bond growth determines whether credit-spread or bank-standard indicators matter more for corporate financing conditions.
insights.quote: If instead bond markets grow because firms borrow more of everything, the balance between the two is unchanged and firms are simply more exposed to both.

insights.claim: Between 1996 and 2019 U.S. bond market growth was mainly credit deepening: bonds rose 9.2% of GDP, total credit to nonfinancial corporates rose from 41% to 52% of GDP (6.6pp of the growth), while the bond share of corporate debt rose only from 57% to 63%.
insights.speaker: Nina Boyarchenko
insights.so_what: Recent U.S. bond growth reflects higher corporate leverage, not banks being displaced, so firms are more exposed to both credit channels.
insights.quote: most of the growth in the size of the corporate bond market in the U.S. between 1996 and 2019 was due to credit deepening

insights.claim: Composition mattered more earlier in the U.S.: between 1980 and 1995, more than 40% of the rise in bonds outstanding (from about 15% to 23.5% of GDP) came from firms shifting from bank loans to market financing.
insights.speaker: Nina Boyarchenko
insights.so_what: The U.S. bank-to-bond substitution was largely an earlier-era story; later growth was leverage-driven.

insights.claim: Across advanced economies pre-pandemic growth mixed composition and credit deepening with large heterogeneity: U.S. and Canada were mostly credit deepening, while New Zealand, Japan and Italy were mostly a shift from bank to market financing.
insights.speaker: Nina Boyarchenko
insights.so_what: In Japan, Italy and New Zealand, bond conditions have genuinely displaced bank standards as a driver of corporate funding.

insights.claim: France and Germany's 1996-2019 bond market growth was roughly half credit deepening and half composition shift, while in the UK credit deepening accounted for about three-fifths.

insights.so_what: Core European markets saw a partial but meaningful move toward bond finance.

insights.claim: Between 2019 and 2021 credit deepened in sixteen of the twenty-four economies studied, making the pandemic primarily a borrowing event despite central bank support aimed at corporate bond markets.
insights.speaker: Nina Boyarchenko
insights.so_what: Pandemic-era policy raised overall corporate leverage rather than mainly shifting firms into bonds.

insights.claim: During the pandemic most Eurozone countries saw nonfinancial corporate debt shift toward bonds, whereas in the U.S. and most other advanced economies the bond share fell as loans grew even faster than bonds.
insights.speaker: Nina Boyarchenko
insights.so_what: Counter to the narrative of bond-market backstops driving U.S. firms to bonds, U.S. loan growth outpaced bonds in 2019-21.
insights.quote: For most of the rest of the advanced economies and for the U.S., instead, the share of bonds in corporate debt declined over the pandemic period, so that loans grew even faster than corporate bonds.

themes.theme: Post-2021 retreat is not a return to banks

insights.claim: From 2021 to 2024 total nonfinancial corporate credit kept growing in nominal terms in every country studied, but GDP grew faster; U.S. corporate bonds rose from $8.0tn to $8.6tn while GDP rose from $23.7tn to $29.4tn.
insights.speaker: Nina Boyarchenko
insights.so_what: The fall in bonds/GDP is a denominator effect from strong nominal growth, not deleveraging via bond paydown.

insights.so_what: In these markets reliance on bonds is intact; lower ratios reflect GDP outgrowing debt.

insights.claim: Conclusions from national accounts depend on where the nonfinancial corporate boundary is drawn, market vs. face valuation of bonds, and which instruments are included; these choices can change not just the size but the direction of the bond-share trend.
insights.speaker: Nina Boyarchenko
insights.so_what: Treat aggregate bond-share trends cautiously; firm-level instrument data is more reliable.

insights.claim: A companion Staff Report combines national accounts with instrument-level data for firms in more than forty countries to show which firms moved toward bonds and how; cross-country differences matter for how credit-boom composition affects the real economy and firms' financing ability.
